title: The Gibeonite Deception
summary: As the kings of Canaan band together against Israel, the people of Gibeon choose another way. Disguised as travelers from a far country, with moldy bread and cracked wineskins, they persuade Israel's leaders to swear a treaty of peace, and Israel does not ask the LORD. When the trick comes to light three days later, Israel keeps its oath, spares the Gibeonites, and makes them woodcutters and water carriers for the congregation and the altar.
story: Jericho has fallen, Achan's sin has been judged, and Ai has been taken. Israel has also renewed the covenant at Mount Ebal, reading the whole law aloud. Now the land responds. Most of its kings choose war, and their coalition will be the subject of the next two chapters. One group chooses surrender by deception. The chapter shows Israel failing in a quieter way than at Ai: not through theft but through trusting its own eyes instead of seeking God. Yet the failure is folded into the LORD's purposes. The treaty with Gibeon triggers the great southern battle of chapter 10, and a Canaanite people, like Rahab's family before them, end up living inside Israel and serving at the LORD's altar.
historical:
Gibeon is securely identified with el-Jib, a site about six miles northwest of Jerusalem. The American archaeologist James B. Pritchard excavated it between 1956 and 1962 and found jar handles inscribed with the city's name, along with a great rock-cut pool and water system from the Iron Age. He found tombs from the Late Bronze Age but little sign of a substantial city from that period, which scholars explain in different ways depending on how they date the conquest and how they read the site's evidence. The other three towns named in verse 17 (Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim) lay nearby in the hills of what became Benjamin and Judah, so the Gibeonites controlled a small league of towns on the central plateau, right in Israel's path.

The treaty had a long afterlife. Gibeon became a Levitical city (Joshua 21:17). Solomon offered sacrifices at the great high place there (1 Kings 3:4). Generations later King Saul tried to wipe out the Gibeonites, and 2 Samuel 21:1-14 traces a famine in David's reign to that broken oath. After the exile, men of Gibeon helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:7). The ark of the covenant later rested for years at Kiriath-jearim (1 Samuel 7:1-2).
cultural:
Treaties in the ancient Near East were solemn and religious. A covenant was sworn by the gods of the parties, and breaking it invited divine punishment. When the Gibeonites say “We are your servants,” they use the language of a vassal seeking protection from a stronger king. That is why the oath binds Israel even after the fraud is uncovered: the leaders swore by the LORD, the God of Israel, and his name could not be treated as a tool to be discarded when inconvenient.

The disguise is aimed at a specific law. Deuteronomy 20:10-18 allowed Israel to offer terms of peace to distant cities but commanded the complete destruction of the peoples of Canaan itself, lest they teach Israel their worship. The Gibeonites seem to know this (verse 24), so they pretend to be from far away. Hauling wood and drawing water were the hardest menial tasks of daily life. Deuteronomy 29:11 already mentions foreigners in Israel's camp who did this work, and here the labor is tied to the house of God and the altar, where large amounts of both were needed.
literary: The chapter is a short, carefully told story of deception and discovery. It opens with a contrast: the kings gather for war (verses 1-2), “But the people of Gibeon” act differently (verse 3). The disguise is described in close detail, then repeated in the Gibeonites' own speech, so the reader sees the props twice. The turning point is a single sentence of narrative judgment: “Then the men of Israel sampled their provisions, but did not seek the counsel of the LORD” (verse 14). The discovery comes after “three days,” and the rest of the chapter works out what an oath means when it was obtained by a lie. The closing formula “to this day” (verse 27) signals that the narrator's readers could still see the Gibeonites serving at the sanctuary.

outline.t: The kings of Canaan unite for war
Israel's questions and the travelers' story
A treaty made without asking the LORD
The trick discovered and the oath kept
Joshua's verdict: servants for the house of God

doctrines.note: Israel's error is not stupidity but self-reliance: they examined the evidence and “did not seek the counsel of the LORD.” The chapter teaches that decisions which look obvious to human judgment still belong under God's guidance.

An oath sworn in the LORD's name binds even when it was obtained by fraud, because it involves God's own name. Israel's faithfulness to a costly promise reflects the character of the God who keeps his covenants.

Like Rahab, the Gibeonites confess that they have heard what the LORD did in Egypt and beyond the Jordan, and they come in fear to seek peace. Their method is dishonest, but their instinct to surrender rather than fight ends with Canaanites living inside Israel and serving at God's altar.

words.note: Berit, covenant or treaty. The same word names God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, and Israel and ordinary agreements between peoples. Israel was forbidden to make a covenant with the peoples of the land (Deuteronomy 7:2), which is exactly what the Gibeonites maneuver them into doing here.

Shaba, to swear an oath. To swear was to call God as witness and guarantor. The leaders' words in verse 19, “We have sworn an oath to them by the LORD,” explain why they cannot simply attack once the lie is exposed.

Ormah, craftiness or shrewdness. The word can be negative (cunning, guile) or positive (prudence, as in Proverbs). Here the Gibeonites act with craft, and the story leaves the reader to weigh both their dishonesty and their clear-eyed recognition that fighting the LORD was hopeless.

Shaal, to ask or inquire. The idiom in verse 14 is literally that they did not ask the mouth of the LORD, meaning they did not inquire of God through the priest and his appointed means (compare Numbers 27:21, where Joshua was to receive guidance through Eleazar the priest).

christ: The link here is a pattern, not a prediction. A people under sentence of judgment come to Israel with nothing but a plea, “We are your servants,” and are spared because of an oath sworn in the LORD's name. Their lives are then bound to the altar. The New Testament speaks of Gentiles who were once far off and strangers to the covenants being brought near (Ephesians 2:12-13), and Hebrews grounds Christian hope in God's promise and oath, two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie (Hebrews 6:17-18). The Gibeonites came by deception; the gospel invites the far-off to come openly. But the story already shows that the God of Israel's covenant makes room for outsiders who turn to him.

hard.q: Why did an oath obtained by lying still bind Israel, and was the curse on the Gibeonites just?
hard.a:
Modern law would treat a contract obtained by fraud as void, and a reader may wonder why Israel did not. The text's answer is that the oath was sworn in the LORD's name, and to break it would profane that name and invite his wrath (verse 20). Later Scripture confirms this reading: when Saul violated the treaty, the land suffered famine (2 Samuel 21:1-2). Some interpreters stress that God used the leaders' mistake to spare people who had turned to him; others stress that the mistake was real and left a Canaanite enclave Israel had been told not to allow.

The servitude imposed on Gibeon is also troubling. Readers note that it was a commutation of a death sentence rather than an added punishment, that the Gibeonites themselves accepted it (verse 25), and that service at the sanctuary brought them close to Israel's worship. Others simply acknowledge that the arrangement reflects the hard social world of the ancient Near East, which the Bible narrates without always endorsing every feature of it.

questions: Israel's leaders trusted what they could see and taste and did not ask God. Where are you most tempted to skip prayer because the answer seems obvious?
The leaders kept a promise that cost them. What makes a promise worth keeping when circumstances change or you discover you were misled?
The Gibeonites chose surrender over war, though they did it dishonestly. What does their story suggest about how God treats people who come to him out of fear?
